profile.reading:
Intergate Seattle West Building B stands at 12201 Tukwila International Boulevard in Tukwila, King County, Washington, a few blocks from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport and roughly half a mile from the South 120th Place cluster of Sabey buildings that public mapping data labels Intergate.East. Building B sits on the Intergate.West side of what Sabey Data Centers now markets as a single combined campus called SDC Seattle, immediately next to Building C at 12101 Tukwila International Boulevard.

Sabey Data Centers is the data center subsidiary of Sabey Corporation, a Puget Sound commercial real estate and construction company founded in 1972 by Dave Sabey that built its early business as a major industrial and office landlord in the Seattle area through the aerospace driven growth of the 1970s and 1980s. Sabey's own company history describes its move into data centers as tracing back to a tenant vacating one of its buildings during the dot com collapse of the early 2000s, leaving the company with an empty large scale technical shell that it recognized as an opportunity in a market starting to demand purpose built computing space. Sabey formalized that pivot in 2010 by partnering with institutional investor National Real Estate Advisors to create Sabey Data Centers as a dedicated operating company, which today describes its national portfolio as more than four million square feet of mission critical space across six campuses in Washington, New York, Texas, and Virginia, with more in development. Whether the original vacated shell that started that pivot was on the Intergate.West side of the Tukwila site, where Building B sits, or on the Intergate.East side a few blocks away, was not established in this pass, since Sabey's current site describes the whole Tukwila property as one campus rather than narrating each building's individual history.

On power and scale, Sabey's own site describes SDC Seattle as a whole, meaning the combined Intergate.East and Intergate.West buildings together, as running on hydroelectric power delivered by Seattle City Light, with more than 90 MVA of aggregate utility power delivered through redundant feeds, backup generators rated at 2.5 MW apiece with 72 hour runtime at peak load, about 9,500 tons of installed HVAC capacity, and over a million square feet of total space across the site. Sabey does not publish a figure specific to the West side of the campus alone, or to Building B individually, so no West campus only or building level IT load, utility power, or generator number is recorded here. Sabey's certifications for the SDC Seattle campus as a whole include HIPAA and HITECH alignment, PCI DSS, SSAE 18 SOC 1 Type 2 and SOC 2 Type 2, LEED Gold, and ISO 27001, again applied at the campus level rather than to individual buildings.

No King County Assessor parcel record, City of Tukwila building permit, or construction and occupancy date specific to Building B was identified in this pass, and no trade press coverage naming this building individually, as opposed to the SDC Seattle campus as a whole, was found either.
profile.capacity_note: not published at the building level. Campus wide total is 54 MW (operator figure) across the Tukwila campus, not applied to this individual building.
profile.research_note: WebSearch was exhausted this session (200 of 200) before this facility group, so research relied on direct WebFetch of Sabey Data Centers' own site plus this database's stored osm_tags, which supplied the confirmed 12201 Tukwila International Boulevard address for this building and 12101 for neighboring Building C. Sabey's current marketing treats the whole Tukwila property as one campus, SDC Seattle, and does not publish separate West-side or per-building capacity figures, so the campus_power_note here is a site-wide figure explicitly flagged as not broken out by East/West, kept distinct in wording from the East campus buildings' note to avoid implying a West-specific number that does not exist. This note is shared identically with sibling West Building C (osm:way/337126739). No King County Assessor or City of Tukwila permit data was accessible in this pass.

profile.campus_power_note: Intergate West / Tukwila International Boulevard side of the combined SDC Seattle campus. Sabey publishes no West-only or per-building capacity figure. Site-wide, per Sabey Data Centers' own site: more than 90 MVA of aggregate utility power delivered through redundant feeds, backup generators rated 2.5 MW apiece with 72 hour runtime at peak load, about 9,500 tons of installed HVAC capacity, and over a million square feet of total space across the whole Tukwila site (both the East and West building clusters combined), not this building or the West side alone.

reading.body:
Sabey Data Centers operates this facility as part of a larger Tukwila campus without publishing power capacity at the individual building level, making its direct contribution to regional AI infrastructure opaque from public sources.

The Intergate Seattle West sub-campus, built in 1999 and spanning roughly 173,000 square feet, is one of two physically separate data center complexes within what operators market as a single Seattle location. The broader Tukwila campus totals 54 megawatts of capacity across multiple buildings, but Sabey does not allocate this power to specific buildings in public disclosures. This opacity is common practice among operators who prefer to market capacity at the campus level rather than expose individual facility utilization or remaining availability.

Sabey's national footprint now spans Washington, Virginia, New York, Texas, and Oregon, with recent growth into the Austin metro region and planned expansion in Oregon. The company's Pacific Northwest campuses, including this one, rely partly on hydroelectric power, which differs materially from the grid dependencies that constrain AI infrastructure in most other regions. This registry tracks only the Washington state facilities, meaning the majority of Sabey's capacity growth lies outside the scope of what this page can show about regional compute concentration.

Without building-level power disclosures, assessing how much capacity supports AI workloads versus other data center tenants remains impossible from available sources. The research status is complete, but completeness here means documenting what is and is not knowable rather than filling gaps with estimates.
